prime.problem: A language model has to say which character is likely to come next. Before any neural net, you need somewhere to keep that knowledge, and a list of 32,033 names doesn't answer "what usually follows m?" by itself.
prime.fits: The names-dataset card turned each name into its bigrams (.e em mm ma a.). This card counts all 228,146 of them into one table, which the next cards turn into probabilities, samples and a loss.
expect: one '.' token for start and end
prime.goal: Build N from names.txt yourself, read any cell or row of it, and explain why one '.' token and a tensor beat a dict with <S>/<E>.

attend: Why does padding each name with '.' at both ends let the same table model first letters and last letters?
Which row and which column of the 28×28 version can never be filled, and why does merging <S> and <E> into one token fix that?
What does the sum of row 0 count, and why must it equal the number of names?
Why do the dict (627 keys) and the tensor (627 nonzero cells) agree exactly?
What happens to the size of the table if the model looks at two previous characters instead of one?

must: Pad each name with '.' on both sides → every name yields len + 1 pairs, including a start pair and an end pair → the one table learns first letters (row 0) and last letters (column 0) along with the inner pairs
Separate <S>/<E> tokens → <E> never starts a pair and <S> never ends one → a full row and column of dead cells (55 of 784) → one shared '.' at index 0 gives a dense 27×27 table
Counts stored as a tensor, not a dict → each row is a vector you can sum or divide in one call → the next cards can turn rows into probabilities and sample from them

The table is indexed by the whole context → each extra character of context multiplies it by 27 (27² = 729, 27³ = 19,683) → most cells are never seen → counting can't scale, which motivates the neural net
elevated: torch.zeros defaults to float32 → counts are stored as dtype=torch.int32 so they stay exact integers; indexing returns a 0-d tensor → use .item() to get a Python int
reference: stoi = {s:i+1 for i,s in enumerate(chars)}; stoi['.'] = 0 and itos as its reverse
zip(chs, chs[1:]) stops at the shorter list

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how the list of names becomes N, and what a row, a column, row 0 and column 0 of N mean. Or draw 'emma' flowing into five cells of the grid.
checklist: pad with '.', zip neighbours into pairs, map characters to indexes with stoi, add 1 to N[ix1, ix2]
row = the current character, column = the one that follows
row 0 = first letters (sums to 32,033 names), column 0 = last letters
one '.' instead of <S>/<E> removes a dead row and column
the counts are the whole model; there are no other parameters

retrieve.q: Explain why the finished count table can be called a trained model, even though no gradient was computed.
answer: the counts are the model's parameters
normalising a row gives the next-character distribution the data implies
training here literally means counting

retrieve.q: Walk 'emma' through the counting loop: list the padded characters, the pairs, their stoi indexes and the cells that change.
answer: pairs .e em mm ma a.
each of those five cells gets += 1

retrieve.q: You want the model to see two previous characters. What does that cost in table size and in data coverage, and why?
answer: the table becomes 27×27×27 = 19,683 cells
only 6,063 of them occur in names.txt, so most contexts have no counts
each extra character multiplies the table by 27 while the data stays fixed

retrieve.q: Why does N[0].sum() equal the number of names, while N.sum() equals the number of bigrams?
answer: every name contributes exactly one start pair (row 0)
every name of length L contributes L + 1 pairs in total
32,033 names → 228,146 pairs

compare.q: Counting fills N in one pass; the neural bigram learns a 27×27 W by gradient descent. What is fundamentally the same, which design choice makes the net slower here, and how does each one fail?
answer: both end up with one row of next-character scores per current character
counting reads the answer straight off the data; the net has to approach it step by step
counting fails on unseen pairs (zeros) and can't grow past short contexts; the net converges slowly on rare rows
the net is worth it because it scales to longer contexts with far fewer parameters

compare.q: This card's table has 729 cells. Why does the same counting idea break down in makemore part 2, and what does that card replace it with?
answer: context of k characters needs 27^k cells
most cells get no data, so counts become zero or noisy
the MLP shares what it learns across contexts through embeddings instead of one cell per context

predict.q: Before checking: does the sum of the m row equal the sum of the m column? What would each of those sums count, and would the answer change in the 28×28 <S>/<E> version?
predict.answer: They are equal: both are 6,642, the number of times m appears in the dataset. Every letter has exactly one character after it (row) and one before it (column), because the padding guarantees a neighbour on both sides. For letters this holds in the 28×28 version too; only the special tokens differ, since <S> has a row but no column and <E> the reverse. With one '.', row 0 and column 0 both sum to 32,033.

apply.task: Extend your counting loop to trigrams: pad each name with two '.' in front and one behind (['.', '.'] + list(w) + ['.']), zip three neighbours, and fill a (27, 27, 27) int32 tensor T. Then check its total and how many cells are nonzero.
apply.done: T.sum() is 228146 (still one tick per predicted character), T[0, 0].sum() is 32033, and (T > 0).sum() is 6063 of 19,683 cells.
apply.hint: for a, b, c in zip(chs, chs[1:], chs[2:]): then T[stoi[a], stoi[b], stoi[c]] += 1.
